A weekly journal of what was designed, built, tested, or debugged during the build semester. Most recent week first — select an entry to expand it.

<Accordion title="Week 8 — 10/12/2026–10/18/2026" subtitle="X-axis motor and belt drive, printed holders, Modbus monitor demo, safety research, first full group test">

**Josué** — Worked on the X-axis motor: he wired it and calibrated it until the movement looked good. He worked out the geometry of the belt path, comparing an oblong layout with an elongated rounded triangle, and evaluated the pros and cons of different types of proximity sensors. He built a small demo interface, with Claude Code, to visualize the Modbus TCP output; it is still a demo, covered by unit tests of its Modbus decoding, and its limits are still being assessed. Following Dr. Socarras's recommendations at the weekly meeting, he also researched safety issues related to the project. In addition, he updated the website and fixed several inconsistencies between the project's artifacts.

**Adriano** — Worked on 3D printing and assembling the prototype that the team tested on Friday. The motor and belt supports were added, along with braces so that the frame no longer wobbles, and the version 4 prototype of the X-axis holder was assembled. He modified and created the adapters for the motor and the belt transmission. He took the feedback from Friday's test and made the corresponding changes, and over the weekend he worked on finishing the Y-axis magnet holder. Version 5 of the X-axis holder is being reprinted with the feedback applied, and this time as a 90% solid part. That makes it much stronger, but it takes significantly longer to print. The stops for the limit switches are ready and will be installed at the start of the following week, and he expects to finish printing the new parts and to test them early that week.

**Group** — The team held a four-hour session that included the first fully functioning test of the system. The movement of both axes was tested successfully. The X axis could almost be considered complete, apart from the limit switches. Only a few steps were skipped, which was largely attributable to the way the belt was temporarily tensioned. The monitor interface built with Claude Code served as a live view of the axes' commanded positions, which allowed the team to verify quickly that the movements were correct. The vertical movement was then tested without the magnet, by holding the ring (nut) on the leadscrew so that it could not rotate, to see the vertical movement. The team also discussed how to place all the electrical components and considered housing them in a box.

<Accordion title="Week 7 — 10/05/2026–10/11/2026" subtitle="Schematic and report restructure, Modbus register test, X-axis belt-drive parts, first look at the full frame, electromagnet test">

**Josué** — Worked mostly on documentation this week. He continued the KiCad schematic, which gives a clearer picture of how the systems connect; the presence (time-of-flight) sensor is not drawn yet. He tested the Modbus registers with `madbus-cli` while the system was not running, and the test confirmed that the code works correctly. He updated the report to the new structure provided in Canvas for the Design document. Chapter 3, the CAD designs, the hardware choices, and the budget were not changed, while the datasheets, software, components no longer used, and power supply sections were refreshed. The proximity sensor, the E-stop, and the fuses are still incomplete or not fully defined. He also made two small code changes: a patch to the Wiznet library and a cleanup of the documentation.

**Adriano** — Continued the 3D CAD work on the X-axis belt-drive parts. He modified the base as agreed, enlarged the transmission piece so that it lines up with the end line of the frame and sits at 180° to the belt, and sketched larger holes so that the frame supports are not rigid or at an angle; in his test, adding 1 mm to the holes gave a perfect fit. He also enlarged the hole that locks a part and prevents it from rotating, from 2 mm to 6 mm, both in the part and in the base. He made an adapter for the ball bearing and the gear, tested it, found that it fits well, and joined the pieces with super glue. This assembly goes into another piece that holds it on the frame, and to keep it from coming out when the belt pulls, he created a cap that fits into the groove of that piece. He is also working on the idea for the Y-axis magnet holder, based on a discussion with Josué and a sketch from last semester.

**Group** — The team saw the full frame together for the first time and noticed that it wobbles slightly; this will be fixed in a following week. They also discussed how to connect the belt and where to place the different steppers and limit switches. They tested the electromagnet by connecting it directly to the 12 V supply with the flyback diode, and it drew about 1.5 A at 12 V DC. The MOSFET driver circuit has not been tested yet.

</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Week 6 — 09/28/2026–10/04/2026" subtitle="KiCad schematic, part-detection options, stepper simulation, vertical assembly printing">

**Josué** — Drew the project's schematic in KiCad: the power supplies (24 V for the motors; 12 V, with a converter down to 5 V, for the electromagnet and the controller), the Nucleo controller, both stepper drivers and motors, the W5500 Ethernet module, the e-stop and start buttons with their status LEDs, the limit switches, and the electromagnet driver. The part-detection sensor is not on it yet. Began comparing part-detection options (a time-of-flight sensor, an ultrasonic sensor, and an IR presence sensor) to choose the best one. Also built a small bench simulation that moves both steppers, with an LED standing in for the electromagnet signal.

<Accordion title="Week 5 — 09/21/2026–09/27/2026" subtitle="Full firmware cycle wired up; open-loop stepper test; frame modeled; electromagnet tested">

**Josué** — Brought the firmware from single test moves to the complete production cycle. All 13 operations of the Home → Pick → Dip → Deposit → Release sequence now run in order, with a start button that restarts the cycle from the beginning and an emergency stop that halts both axes while keeping the electromagnet engaged. Along the way, fixed the emergency-stop and start buttons being read with inverted logic, and did a cleanup pass on the stepper driver and motion planner that removed unused code and made invalid states impossible to represent. The wiring and pinout documentation was also brought up to date. Toward the end of the week, began the next round of firmware work (Modbus parameter mapping, fault reporting, and homing on the limit switches) and started updating the software section of the Senior Design report, including its flowcharts, to match the current design.

Also tested the movement of one stepper motor with open-loop positioning (no position feedback), and the result was really promising.

**Adriano** — Turned the X- and Y-axis movement concept discussed with Josué into a full-scale 3D design, built from real dimensions and the actual frame components. Added two supported linear rails and four sliding bearing blocks to the frame model, then began designing the plate that connects the bearing blocks to the rest of the moving assembly, including measured screw locations and countersunk mounting holes. Checking how the frame, rails, blocks, and plate fit together in 3D showed where the next work is: detailing the connections between the moving components so the mechanism can be assembled and tested for real.

**Group** — Got together to test the electromagnet and finish measuring its electrical properties. Measured its resistance experimentally and, from that, estimated its current draw at 1.2 A; 1.5 A will be budgeted to leave some headroom. Also tested its strength qualitatively with a hammer. A hammer isn't representative of the parts we'll be handling, since it covers little of the magnet's face, but the magnet still held it with impressive strength.

</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Week 4 — 09/14/2026–09/20/2026" subtitle="First MCU-to-stepper test passes; movement systems modeled">

**Josué** — Finally assembled the 24 V power supply and calibrated its output voltage to 24.1 V. Connected the power supply to the stepper driver, the MCU to the stepper driver, and the stepper motor to the stepper driver. Tested the stepper movement code by having the motor turn 10 times and land in the same place successfully. Because the stepper driver code overshot slightly, implemented a landing speed variable (what is usually called creep speed on elevators, a common technique) so the motor arrives smoothly at its destination without overshooting. This was the first successful MCU-to-stepper test.

Also researched 5 V communication with the STM32, since its logic is 3.3 V. Found that the STM32 has FT (five-volt tolerant) pins, and devised a common-anode, open-drain configuration that allows communication with the stepper driver.

**Adriano** — Worked on the 3D model for the horizontal and vertical movement of the project, including how both systems will attach to the main frame. The horizontal movement design consists of a bearing connected to a set of 3D-printed gears. The inner part of the bearing will be attached to a cylindrical section that extends from the main base for the sliders. This design will allow the mechanism to move horizontally while staying supported by the main structure, and the gears will transfer motion to the horizontal assembly.

For the vertical movement, the design uses two holders with bearings to support the lead screw and connect it to the main base. A brass threaded piece on the lead screw will hold the central section of the magnet holder. As the lead screw rotates, the brass piece will move vertically and carry the magnet holder with it. Side sliders placed around the magnet holder will guide its movement and help keep the magnet aligned and attached to the rest of the structure during operation.

</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Week 3 — 09/07/2026–09/13/2026" subtitle="Website rebuild while supply-blocked; vertical movement redesign">

**Josué** — Was supply-blocked on firmware work: the stepper motor and controller were on hand, but the power supply order ran into issues. Used the time to rebuild the website from scratch with better navigation, the same content, and clearer readability.

**Adriano** — Continued taking measurements and used them to modify the 3D design. Printed a draft of the plastic field base and developed a mechanism to transfer the horizontal motion to the base. Also redesigned the vertical movement system, including a new 3D-printed component for the lead screw assembly, allowing the motor's rotational motion to be converted into vertical linear movement. Throughout the process, verified that all components could properly connect and, when necessary, designed adapters or custom 3D-printed solutions to ensure compatibility.

</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Week 2 — 08/31/2026–09/06/2026" subtitle="Linear rails installed; component sourcing">

**Josué** — Researched how to map the project's various elements to a Modbus-compatible memory layout.

**Adriano** — Focused on taking measurements and installing the linear rails onto the base frame. Also identified and obtained the additional components needed for the assembly, while verifying that the parts would properly fit and integrate with the overall structure.

</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Week 1 — 08/24/2026–08/30/2026" subtitle="Motion control validated on hardware; frame assembly begins">

**Josué** — The complete two-axis motion control software was already in place, including Modbus TCP communication, acceleration/deceleration motion planning, operation sequencing, and end-effector control. The software architecture had grown to approximately 1,200 lines across 23 files. However, although the motion control stack had been implemented, the stepper motor pulse generation had not yet been validated on the actual hardware.

This week, the stepper driver was successfully tested and confirmed to generate pulses at the correct frequency and timing. A critical race condition affecting the channel arm/disarm logic was identified and corrected, and the driver now supports both position and velocity control through a unified speed-ramp interface. Temporary motion-control workarounds were also replaced with production-ready abstractions, while the existing motion planner and sequencer required no major changes. Emergency-stop and start-button inputs were integrated into the sequencer, and its internal state logic was simplified to improve reliability and maintainability.

**Adriano** — Focused on gathering and organizing the mechanical components required for the system. He ordered most of the necessary parts online, reviewed the dimensions, and began assembling the main aluminum frame. Initial measurements were taken to verify the overall structure and ensure the components could be positioned correctly before continuing with the final assembly.

Over the weekend, he continued working on the mechanical structure by cutting excess aluminum extrusion and resizing sections of the frame to the required dimensions. He also began attaching the linear rails to the main frame, establishing the mechanical foundation that will support the motion system and the remaining components.

</Accordion>
